UK parliamentary sentences, coded for sentiment on a six-level scale

parlasent.Rd

A hundred sentences from ParlaSent 1.0 (Mochtak et al. 2023), the English training file, drawn from UK parliamentary proceedings and annotated by two coders with a reconciliation pass. It is the package's exclusive-choice corpus and the only one whose labels collide.

Usage

parlasent

Format

A tibble with 100 rows and 19 columns.

  • id is the document identifier, uk_001 to uk_100.

  • sentence is the document, 11 to 32 words, median 22.

  • label is the three-level reconciled sentiment. Factor, Negative, Neutral, Positive.

  • reconciliation is the six-level reconciled code. Factor, ordered from Negative through Positive.

  • annotator1 and annotator2 are the two independent six-level codings.

  • name is the member speaking. 93 distinct across the hundred.

  • party is the party affiliation. Eight parties.

  • gender is the recorded gender of the member.

  • ruling says whether the member sat with the government or the opposition.

  • date is the date of the sitting, 2015-01-08 to 2021-02-23.

  • term is the parliamentary term.

  • document_id and sentence_id are ParlaSent internal identifiers.

  • split is the authors' own train, dev, and test partition. This sample crosses all three, since nothing here is trained.

  • stratum_N is the size of the six-level stratum in the source file.

  • stratum_n is the number drawn from it.

  • weight is stratum_N / stratum_n, for weighting back at the six-level stratum.

  • weight3 is the same pooled to the three-level class.

Source

Mochtak, M., Rupnik, P., Meden, K., and Ljubesic, N. (2023). The multilingual sentiment dataset of parliamentary debates ParlaSent 1.0. Slovenian language resource repository CLARIN.SI. https://hdl.handle.net/11356/1868

Distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, unlike the rest of this package. See LICENSE.note. Drawn from the English training file with seed 444.

Details

Normalized for scoring, Negative and Neutral both begin with N. Prefix matching cannot tell them apart, since a split label often emits only its first character, so instrument() refuses to build this label set that way and it can only be scored with exact = TRUE and a live backend. The collision is a property of a published coding scheme rather than something constructed to demonstrate one.

The annotators worked six levels and the three-level label is their collapse. Both mixed levels fold to their own polarity, so Neutral means no sentiment content and nothing else. Ambiguity lives in M_Positive and M_Negative, which are inside the positive and negative classes rather than beside them.

levelmeaning
Positiveentirely or predominantly positive
M_Positiveambiguous or mixed, leaning positive
P_Neutralno sentiment content, leaning positive
N_Neutralno sentiment content, leaning negative
M_Negativeambiguous or mixed, leaning negative
Negativeentirely or predominantly negative

Sampling

Stratified on the six levels rather than on the three, seed 444. Seventeen each of Positive, Negative, P_Neutral, and N_Neutral, and sixteen each of the two mixed levels, giving 33 negative, 34 neutral, and 33 positive.

Sampling on the collapse would have let the draw decide the mix inside each class, and nothing would record which mix arrived. The neutral levels matter most. P_Neutral outnumbers N_Neutral 413 to 267 in the source, so a proportional draw would give a neutral class that leans positive, and a model answering that lean would look biased when the sample was.

The mixed levels are kept rather than dropped. They are the only sentences that give margin and prob_other anything to separate. A corpus of unambiguous cases returns saturated on every row and every uncertainty diagnostic has nothing to show.

Class balance

The source file is 48.8 percent negative, 26.2 percent neutral, and 25.0 percent positive, against 33, 34, and 33 here. Recall, specificity, and AUC are computed within a class and carry over. Accuracy, precision, F1, and kappa move with the class mix and do not. weight3 reweights to the source proportions, and weight does the same at the six-level stratum, though at a higher cost in precision. The effective sample size is about 90 using weight3 and about 69 using weight.

The sample is also deliberately harder than the file it came from. Mixed levels are 32 percent here against 14.6 percent there.

The human ceiling

annotator1 and annotator2 are the two independent codings before reconciliation, so the corpus carries its own benchmark. On these hundred sentences the two coders agree with each other on 0.720, which is 0.765 on the four unambiguous levels, 0.625 on the two mixed ones, and 0.570 on the raw six. Across the full 2,600-sentence file they agree on 0.783, and on the raw six levels 0.660.

A model is worth reading against 0.720 rather than against 1. The gap between the pure and mixed figures is what the uncertainty diagnostics should track.

References

Kuzman Pungersek, T., Ljubesic, N., Erjavec, T., et al. (2025). Linguistically annotated multilingual comparable corpora of parliamentary debates ParlaMint-en.ana 5.0. CLARIN.SI. https://hdl.handle.net/11356/2006

Mochtak, M., Rupnik, P., and Ljubesic, N. (2024). The ParlaSent multilingual training dataset for sentiment identification in parliamentary proceedings. Proceedings of LREC-COLING 2024, 16024-16036.

Examples

data(parlasent)
table(parlasent$reconciliation, parlasent$label)
#>             
#>              Negative Neutral Positive
#>   Negative         17       0        0
#>   M_Negative       16       0        0
#>   N_Neutral         0      17        0
#>   P_Neutral         0      17        0
#>   M_Positive        0       0       16
#>   Positive          0       0       17

# The two coders before reconciliation, on the raw six levels.
mean(parlasent$annotator1 == parlasent$annotator2)
#> [1] 0.57
